summary: The build can start now: the machine has Python, pip, Node/npx, Docker, the documentdb MCP data-plane server, and a comprehensive set of documentdb-* skills installed. The main gaps are: an LLM credential/provider is not present (required by the LangChain scoring/explainer agents), a few nonessential developer accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit, local DocumentDB container) are not installed/started, and several cold-answer facts were outdated or mixed up with Cosmos DB or other products and must be corrected before code is written. Nothing critical is missing that prevents implementing the sample against the provided cluster, but the builder must follow the corrected facts below.
summary_points: All required runtime tools for coding and verifying against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster are present (python, pip, node/npx, docker) and the documentdb MCP server is available for data‑plane verification.

Key DocumentDB facts in the cold answers were mixed with Cosmos DB and other products (resource type, CLI command group, connection-string form, auth, vector & full-text search). The builder must use the DocumentDB (mongoClusters) model and the DocumentDB docs listed below.

An LLM credential/provider is not in the inventory and is required by the LangChain scoring and explainer agents; obtain and supply it (OPENAI_API_KEY or an Azure OpenAI deployment) before running end-to-end.
Helpful accelerators are missing (DocumentDB Agent Kit and an optionally-running local DocumentDB container). They are not blocking but would speed development and testing.

The installed documentdb-* skills and the documentdb MCP server provide the data-plane commands and design guidance needed to create collections, indexes, run explains, and verify write-back; use them for verification.

Some implementation details are still unspecified in the prompt (exact applicant schema, LLM model, seeded test dataset); these are listed as information gaps the builder must decide or ask the author about.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for accounts: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (and nested child resources for databases/collections such as Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and /mongodbCollections).
confusions.grounded_answer: Current managed MongoDB clusters (vCore offering) are deployed as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters). Use mongoClusters for Bicep/ARM/Terraform and the az documentdb/az cosmosdb command groups that target clusters. The older databaseAccounts resource shape (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) describes Cosmos DB account resources and the Cosmos DB multi-tenant account model — not the vCore mongoClusters resource.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM / templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical overlap: Cosmos DB account resource types (databaseAccounts) are the old multi-tenant model and share the DocumentDB name; the newer vCore managed MongoDB offering uses a new resource type (mongoClusters).

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and the Cosmos DB account model in IaC or CLI calls would attempt to create/manage the wrong resource type or use different CLI commands; the builder would fail to create or inspect the vCore mongo cluster and might create Cosmos accounts instead.
improvements: Add a prominent note on the DocumentDB quickstart and agent skill docs explaining that the vCore managed MongoDB product uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts) and link the ARM/Bicep schema pages.
Update the agent-kit skill README to surface the correct resource type when generating IaC templates for clusters (use mongoClusters).

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create a Mongo-capable account: az cosmosdb create ...; if not available install the cosmosdb extension (az extension add --name azure-cosmosdb-preview).
confusions.grounded_answer: The active commands for managed MongoDB clusters are under the documentdb command group (az documentdb mongocluster ...). There are cosmosdb subcommands for Cosmos DB multi-tenant accounts, and some CLI docs show az cosmosdb mongodb database/collection commands, but the cluster-level managed MongoDB (vCore) operations use az documentdb mongocluster (documentdb extension).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Name overlap across CLI groups and reused subcommands for different Cosmos/MongoSKUs; older Cosmos DB Mongo API docs use az cosmosdb, which caused the model to conflate the two.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create or the wrong CLI commands may create or manage a Cosmos multi-tenant account rather than the managed mongoClusters resource; verification steps or automation calling the wrong command group will fail.
improvements: Document example CLI invocations for common developer tasks in the sample README using az documentdb mongocluster so builders don't run az cosmosdb accidentally.
Add a one-line clarification in the prompt/skill.md: "Use az documentdb mongocluster for vCore clusters."

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@<apiVersion> (for the account). Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore managed MongoDB offering you should use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep) and the corresponding Azure resource types exposed via AzAPI/AzureRM provider modules (the AVM/res/document-db/mongo-cluster module). The older databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource applies to Cosmos DB multi-tenant accounts, not mongoClusters vCore resources.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM / templates)
Azure Verified Module: Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Similar resource-provider namespace and long-standing usage of Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB created confusion between account-based deployments and the newer vCore mongoClusters resource.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder generates IaC targeting databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account the template will target the wrong product SKU and either fail to deploy or create a different service type. Use mongoClusters resource type for vCore clusters.
improvements: Add a short example in the sample repo README showing the exact Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters Bicep snippet to use when IaC is required.
If the sample explicitly forbids provisioning (as here), ensure the README explains why IaC isn't used and link to the correct AVM module for later reference.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the MongoDB URI form (TLS required). Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myaccount@ or mongodb+srv://...; TLS port 10255 when using explicit host:port; required options ssl/tls=true, replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (managed mongoClusters) connection URIs differ from Cosmos DB's older Mongo API URIs. For the managed vCore cluster and the local gateway the documented host ports start at 10260 (gateway) and SRV hostnames use *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com. Local gateway example: mongodb://<admin>:<pw>@localhost:10260/?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true. For cluster SRV URIs use mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false (or MONGODB-OIDC for Entra auth), and query-port ranges start at 10260 for nodes when "query from any node" is enabled. Do not assume the cosmos.azure.com:10255 format (that's from older Cosmos DB multi-tenant platform).

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: DocumentDB local gateway (development-loop)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer described the older Cosmos DB (multi-tenant) Mongo API connection string and ports (10255) rather than the DocumentDB/vCore gateway and cluster ports (10260+), and mixed SRV hostnames between products.

confusion_sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell
Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port (10255 vs 10260) or the wrong auth parameters will result in connection failures. The builder must read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment and use the exact supplied connection string for the cluster.
improvements: Add an explicit connection-string example in the sample's .env.example that uses mongodb+srv with the cluster's mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com host and documents the correct port and authMechanism for native and Entra auth.
Note in the README to never hardcode or print the actual DOCUMENTDB_URI and to use the MCP list-connection-strings for verification.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB primarily bills throughput as RUs/sec with provisioned/autoscale/serverless. There is also a separate managed MongoDB offering/compute tiers (vCore-style SKUs such as M-series like M30) billed differently; in practice expect RUs for Cosmos multi-tenant accounts and vCore/compute tiers for managed MongoDB instances.
confusions.grounded_answer: Both models exist but they apply to different product SKUs. The vCore managed MongoDB offering (mongoClusters) uses compute tiers such as M30, M40 (vCore-like SKUs) and storage/compute choices (as shown in sample CLI and Bicep parameters). The older Cosmos DB multi-tenant accounts use RUs for throughput. For this sample (the run environment supplies an M30 cluster), expect vCore-tier billing and sizing rather than RU billing.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Confusion arises because Cosmos DB (multi-tenant) historically uses RUs while the relatively new vCore-managed MongoDB product uses M-series tiers; both fall under the broader 'DocumentDB/Cosmos' family.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU-based scaling it might try to create or configure throughput settings that aren't applicable to a vCore cluster, causing provisioning or configuration errors.
improvements: Document in the sample's README that the provided dev cluster is vCore (M30) and that the sample must not attempt to configure RU throughput for it.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB API clients typically authenticate with SCRAM username/password or Cosmos account primary/secondary keys. Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID) is not generally available for the MongoDB wire API in most Cosmos DB deployments.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB managed MongoDB clusters support Native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication. You can enable Microsoft Entra ID on the cluster (authConfig.allowedModes includes MicrosoftEntraID) and register Microsoft Entra principals as cluster admin or non-administrative users; drivers connect using authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and supply an OIDC token (example patterns and Azure Identity token callback implementations are documented for Python).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
How to connect (Python OIDC example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected historic limitations of some Cosmos DB Mongo API variants and general uncertainty about AD support; the vCore mongoClusters explicitly support Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) and document how to enable and use it.

confusion_sources.title: Enable Microsoft Entra ID authentication (az documentdb mongocluster update)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is unsupported they might implement only SCRAM and miss a recommended secure path for production authentication, or they might try to reuse account keys where Entra ID identities should be used. For samples that demonstrate Entra-based auth, missing the correct mechanics will break connections.
improvements: Add a short example in the sample README showing how to enable Microsoft Entra ID auth on the cluster and a Python snippet using azure.identity.DefaultAzureCredential and the pymongo OIDC callback (link to the Python example).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers for your language (for Python use pymongo). Do not use the azure-cosmos SDK for MongoDB access — use the MongoDB-compatible driver.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Use the official MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python) to interact with Azure DocumentDB managed MongoDB clusters; the samples and quickstarts use pymongo and show connection examples. There is no separate DocumentDB-specific runtime SDK for MongoDB data-plane operations — use MongoDB drivers plus the DocumentDB management CLI/ARM types for control-plane tasks.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no widely available native vector-indexing DSL in classic Azure Cosmos DB/MongoDB API; creating ANN is provider-specific and not standard.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the managed vCore DocumentDB clusters the service advertises native vector-indexing capabilities (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF). DocumentDB provides provider-specific index creation options (e.g., createIndex with type "cosmosSearch" or vendor-specific options) and has a Python quickstart that shows creating and using vector indexes. The cold answer describes older Cosmos limitations; the current vCore product supports built-in ANN index types as documented in the vector-search quickstart.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Vector index with Python in Azure DocumentDB
documentdb-vector-search skill

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer reflected classic Cosmos DB limitations; newer vCore clusters add provider-specific vector indexes and commands.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Vector index with Python in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes vectors are not supported they may implement an external vector store or mismatched embedding dims; if they assume a standard Mongo vector index DSL they'll get commands that don't exist. Use the DocumentDB vector index docs and the documentdb-vector-search skill guidance.
improvements: Add an example in the sample README showing the exact createIndex/createSearchIndexes command to create a vector index for the embedding dims chosen by the sample's LLM/embedding model.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search (or another search service). Cosmos DB doesn't provide a first-class integrated full-text engine comparable to Azure Cognitive Search.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is outdated for the DocumentDB vCore clusters: DocumentDB provides a built-in full-text search engine (createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage, BM25 ranking) and supports hybrid retrieval (BM25 keyword indexes plus vector indexes) with example workflows (RRF fusion). Azure Cognitive Search is an option, but DocumentDB's integrated $search and createSearchIndexes are the documented path for in-cluster full-text and hybrid search.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB
Hybrid search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos and other flavors required external search services; the vCore DocumentDB product now includes built-in full-text search and hybrid search capabilities — the cold answer described older constraints.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder chooses to pipeline documents to Azure Cognitive Search they add unnecessary architecture and complexity; conversely, assuming $search exists but not enabling preview features will cause confusion. The sample should use createSearchIndexes and $search when a text index is needed.
improvements: In the sample README, state explicitly whether the sample uses built-in $search (and how to enable it) or an external search index; include the createSearchIndexes snippet if $search is used.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported versions vary; historically Cosmos DB supported older MongoDB API versions (3.6, 4.x); check configured server version. Some server-side JS, some aggregation stages, transactions and change streams were limited in older API versions.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) supports multiple MongoDB wire-protocol versions including 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 depending on cluster configuration. The service publishes a MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility matrix showing operator and stage support per server version. Many common features are supported, but you must consult the compatibility matrix for specific operators. Use the compatibility guide to confirm whether a specific operator or command is supported for the configured server-version.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer was vague and referred to older limitations; the DocumentDB compatibility matrix provides exact operator-by-version support and the product now advertises support for recent wire-protocol versions.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes features are missing they might avoid useful aggregation stages (or vice versa). The sample should check the cluster's server version (inventory/skill_md said 7.0) and consult the compatibility page for any borderline operator used by the sample.
improvements: Add a single-line step in sample verification: `client.server_info()` or an MCP explain call to record the server version and then reference the compatibility page for any advanced operator used.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use DocumentDB local or a local MongoDB container; DocumentDB gateway on 10260 for the DocumentDB local image and tls=true & tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The DocumentDB local gateway Docker image is ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local and exposes gateway port 10260. The documented local connection string example uses mongodb://<admin>:<pw>@localhost:10260/?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true. The sample run environment specifically disallows running a local gateway for verification (it instructs to verify against the live cluster), but the local image is the correct developer accelerator if chosen.

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: DocumentDB local gateway (development-loop)

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB exposes Change Feed; the MongoDB-style changeStreams interface is not universally supported on all Mongo API versions; use Cosmos Change Feed otherwise.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style changeStreams (the compatibility matrix marks $changeStream as supported across versions) and also provides the Cosmos Change Feed semantics. However, exact behavior and supported details depend on the server version and cluster configuration; consult the MQL compatibility page. You do not necessarily need to enable a separate toggle beyond having a compatible server version.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described older Cosmos DB limitations and conflated Cosmos Change Feed with MongoDB changeStreams support; current vCore clusters list changeStreams/$changeStream among supported stages in the compatibility matrix.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes changeStreams are not available they might implement an external polling pattern instead of using a native changeStream, adding complexity.
improvements: Add a verification step in the sample README: run a small changeStream sample against a test collection and include the compatibility check for the cluster's server version.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (service-specific) for data-plane inspection and MongoDB-specific tools. The general Azure MCP server covers generic Azure resource management but the documentdb MCP provides DB-level commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The documentdb MCP server provides the data-plane commands (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, explain_operation, etc.) and should be used for all database inspection and verification. The general azure MCP server exists for control-plane tasks but it doesn't replace the documentdb data-plane tools.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally shipped a service named Azure DocumentDB, which evolved and was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB. The Cosmos DB MongoDB API implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top of the Cosmos DB engine. The open-source project named DocumentDB is unrelated.
confusions.grounded_answer: Broadly correct but easily misread: Microsoft used the DocumentDB name historically and Cosmos DB later became the umbrella brand. The managed MongoDB vCore product and the older Cosmos DB Mongo API share heritage but are distinct SKUs; the open-source DocumentDB project exists and is separate. Because of these renames and overlaps, many docs and samples still use legacy names—builders should prefer the current product names (DocumentDB for the vCore managed MongoDB cluster resource and 'Cosmos DB' for account-model services) and consult the product docs linked here.

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas

improvements: Add a short 'naming clarification' paragraph in the sample README explaining the differences between "DocumentDB (managed Mongo vCore)", "Cosmos DB (multi-tenant)" and Amazon DocumentDB to prevent builder confusion.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is Azure Cosmos DB (Microsoft's engine) when using the Cosmos MongoDB API — not the native MongoDB server. That means you use standard MongoDB drivers but some server-side behavior differs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo) for data-plane access, but test queries and operators against the actual cluster because engine behavior and feature parity differ in some operators and management commands. Use the MQL compatibility matrix and run client server_info() to check the cluster server version when implementing advanced queries.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for this sample; include only if you will ship Terraform-based IaC. If desired, install Terraform and the azurerm provider; the Azure Verified Module (AVM) exists for mongo clusters.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Helpful for interactive debugging and manual verification of queries and indexes; install mongosh so developers can run ad hoc checks (or rely on the documentdb MCP server). Example: install mongosh from MongoDB downloads.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

inventory_recommendations.name: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit)
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: This accelerator bundles agent-ready skills and templates that speed sample creation (index examples, seed scripts, playbooks). Install with: npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit. If not installing, ensure the README describes how to perform its common tasks manually.
